opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was just the density. You walk around that part of Haidian, near Tsinghua and Peking University, and it feels a bit like Palo Alto compressed into a few blocks. You've got labs, startups, and big-tech research offices basically sharing the same coffee shops, and a huge share of the people building these models came out of the same couple of university programs. So the talent pipeline is incredibly short: someone finishes a PhD, walks across the street, and they're training frontier-scale models a few months later.

The second thing was the culture around openness. A lot of these teams are releasing open-weight models, and they're doing it with real technical seriousness: detailed reports, strong engineering on efficiency, very pragmatic choices about compute. When you're more constrained on hardware, you get very good at squeezing performance out of what you have, and you can feel that mindset in the conversations. People talk less about grand AGI narratives and more about "how do we make training cheaper, how do we make inference faster, how do we get this into products."

And the third thing, which I think people in the US underestimate, is the speed and intensity. The work ethic is real, the iteration cycles are fast, and there's a lot of mutual awareness. Everyone knows what the lab down the street released last week. That competitive pressure, plus a shared talent pool, creates a kind of flywheel that reminds me of what the Bay Area felt like in the early deep learning days.

For me as someone who works on open models and post-training, it was a bit humbling. It made clear that the open ecosystem isn't a US-centered story anymore. Some of the most important open releases are coming out of that neighborhood, and if we in the West care about open AI research, we need to take that seriously, both as competition and as a community we're learning from.

r001.rationale: The response compares the dense cluster near Tsinghua and Peking University to “Palo Alto compressed into a few blocks” and later likens its startup dynamics to the Bay Area.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most was the density. You have Tsinghua, Peking University, and then within a couple of kilometers in Zhongguancun and Wudaokou you have Zhipu, Moonshot, Baichuan, and a dozen smaller labs, and a lot of the people running them studied together or overlapped at the same handful of research groups. It felt like Palo Alto around Stanford in the early days, but compressed even tighter, and with the university much more directly in the loop. Professors are co-founders, grad students are moving between labs and companies constantly, and the talent flow is incredibly fast.

The second thing was how much of the conversation was about open weights. In the US, open models are kind of a side strategy for most labs, something Meta does and everyone else tolerates. There, releasing weights is close to the default. Part of that is practical, since compute constraints mean they cannot just out-scale the frontier labs, so they compete on distribution and on being the thing everyone builds on. But part of it is also a genuine research culture that came out of those university groups. People were very candid about what worked and what did not, in a way I honestly do not always get in San Francisco.

And the third thing, which I think gets underappreciated, is that these teams are very young and very pragmatic. The question was never whether a given technique is elegant. It was whether it ships and whether it holds up on the benchmarks people actually care about. That mindset combined with that talent density is why I think the gap people assume between the US and Chinese open model ecosystems is a lot smaller than the headlines suggest.

r001.rationale: The response compares the dense Beijing startup cluster to Palo Alto around Stanford, saying it felt similar but even more compressed.

astra-6.text: What struck me was how geographically concentrated it was. You have Tsinghua as a source of talent, and then this cluster of AI startups nearby. It brings to mind the relationship between Stanford and Silicon Valley: a university can be an anchor for a whole ecosystem. Proximity makes it easier for people and ideas to move between research and companies.

r001.rationale: The response compares the Tsinghua startup cluster to Stanford and Silicon Valley, describing a nearby university as an anchor for an ecosystem.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was the density of talent. You have researchers, founders, and engineers all concentrated around the university, so ideas and people can move between teams very quickly. It reminded me of what makes Silicon Valley work: it’s not just one great company or one great university, but the network around them. I’d be careful about drawing a sweeping conclusion from that, but the concentration itself was striking.

r001.rationale: The response compares the concentrated talent and network around Tsinghua with what makes Silicon Valley work, conveying a comparison to the Bay Area.
